Nature communications 2026 2026-11-05 2026-11-05 In recent years, record-breaking heatwaves have occurred over many regions of the Earth causing serious impacts to human and natural systems. Here we show that recently observed exceptional heatwaves are no match to potential future 21 st  century events based on multiple metrics. For several observed heatwaves, this holds even under low- and medium-emissions scenarios. In a high- to very high-emissions future, many regions are projected to experience heatwaves that generate several times more cumulative heat and are many times longer (up to several months) than the observed heatwaves. Should the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement not be implemented, in most regions a concerningly large proportion of projected heatwaves exceeds all analyzed heatwave characteristics at once. Our results underscore the crucial need for substantial emissions reduction and have important implications for adaptation measures, as a substantial proportion of projected heatwaves is well outside the recent lived experience.

In recent years, record-breaking heatwaves have occurred over many regions of the Earth causing serious impacts to human and natural systems. Here we show that recently observed exceptional heatwaves are no match to potential future 21st century events based on multiple metrics. For several observed heatwaves, this holds even under low- and medium-emissions scenarios. In a high- to very high-emissions future, many regions are projected to experience heatwaves that generate several times more cumulative heat and are many times longer (up to several months) than the observed heatwaves. Should the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement not be implemented, in most regions a concerningly large proportion of projected heatwaves exceeds all analyzed heatwave characteristics at once. Our results underscore the crucial need for substantial emissions reduction and have important implications for adaptation measures, as a substantial proportion of projected heatwaves is well outside the recent lived experience.

This paper shows that current temperature and emission-reduction targets provide only limited protection against future heatwaves, which are found to surpass recent exceptional events across multiple regions of the world.

Regions with reference heatwaves reaching exceptionally high median severity values (Northern Africa & Middle East, South America, and Southern Africa; see Table 2 and methods), have a projected exceedance likelihood of approximately 1-in-8 to 1-in-6 heatwaves under SSP1-2.6 (Supplementary Data 9 ), which increases to approximately 27% in South America and Southern Africa and 36% in Northern Africa & Middle East under SSP3-7.0 (Supplementary Data 10 ). Australia and China, which both experienced peak-median-severity heatwaves in 2019 and 2022 (Table 2 ), respectively, are projected to exceed the median severity of the observed event in 3% and 0.5% of future heatwaves under SSP1-2.6 (Supplementary Data 9 ). These relatively low exceedance percentages highlight the exceptional median severity of these events. However, under high-emissions conditions (SSP3-7.0), the chances of exceeding the median severity of the two observed heatwaves increases to approximately 12% in Australia and 3% in China (Supplementary Data 10 ). This means that the chances of surpassing the reference heatwave are nearly 5-times and 8-times as high, respectively, under high-emissions conditions compared to a low-emissions future. Under SSP1-2.6, most regions (China, Europe, Northern Africa & Middle East, Pacific Northwestern USA & Canada, and South America) show a 10% chance to reach a median heatwave severity of at least 2 (Supplementary Data 11 ), which means that the average heatwave-day reaches temperatures where the difference to the climatological mean is twice as large as the difference between climatology and extreme heat threshold (Tx90p). Under SSP3-7.0, these chances more than double. Furthermore, under these conditions Australia and India & Pakistan show projected chances of 10% to reach median heatwave severity values of 2 (Supplementary Data 12 ). Heatwaves with exceptionally high median severity relative to Tx99p occurred in Australia, China, and Northern Africa & Middle East (Supplementary Data 8 ). Whereas the exceedance percentage in China is limited to 2% in a low-emissions future (SSP1-2.6), the chances are approximately 1-in-5 heatwaves in Australia and Northern Africa & Middle East (Supplementary Data 13 ). Under SSP3-7.0, these chances increase substantially: approximately 8% of projected heatwaves in China and close to 40% in Australia and Northern Africa & Middle East exceed the exceptionally high median severity of the observed reference heatwave relative to the respective region’s 99 th percentile (Supplementary Data 14 ). For China, the chances of exceeding the peak-spatial-extent are still 2% under SSP3-7.0 (Supplementary Data 16 ), again highlighting the exceptionality of the event. This, nevertheless, represents a 14-times increase in exceedance likelihood compared to low-emissions conditions. Under low-emissions conditions (SSP1-2.6), in five of the nine regions (Australia, China, India & Pakistan, Northern Africa & Middle East, and Southern Africa) at least 1-in-10 heatwaves reaches a median heatwave area of 50% (Supplementary Data 17 ). This means that those heatwaves on average cover more than half of the region with extreme local heat. These chances more than double under SSP3-7.0 (Supplementary Data 18 ). For four of those regions, the chances even more than triple (Supplementary Data 18 ). Even under a strong mitigation scenario (SSP1-2.6), projections show heatwave lengths up to several months, with five out of nine regions (Europe, Northeast Siberia, Northern Africa & Middle East, Pacific Northwestern USA & Canada, and South America) showing heatwaves approaching or even hitting the theoretical maximum length of six consecutive months (see Methods). Moreover, exceptionally long observed heatwaves in Australia, China, Europe, India & Pakistan, Northeast Siberia, and Northern Africa & Middle East (Table 2 ) are outmatched by projected events, even when strong emissions mitigation occurs. While exceedance percentages in Australia and China are limited to 4%, between 6% and 11% of projected heatwaves in Europe, India & Pakistan, and Northern Africa & Middle East and approximately 1-in-4 projected heatwaves in Northeast Siberia exceed the exceptionally long reference events (Supplementary Data 19 ). These proportions increase substantially under SSP3-7.0 (Supplementary Data 20 ). In Australia and China, this results in an exceedance likelihood of approximately 1-in-10. Furthermore, close to 1-in-5 heatwaves in Europe and India & Pakistan, 1-in-4 in Northern Africa & Middle East and 1-in-3 in Northeast Siberia are projected to last longer than the exceptionally long reference events (Supplementary Data 20 ). In Australia, China, and Northern Africa & Middle East, this would mean chances of exceeding the reference events ~3- to 4-times as high as under SSP1-2.6. Under high-emission scenarios (Fig. 2 ), Australia is the only region with a possible maximum heatwave length of less than six months (Australia only reaches the six-month limit under CMIP6 SSP5-8.5 and CMIP5 RCP8.5, see Supplementary Figs. 22 & 37 ). This means that without significant emissions reduction, the other regions might experience sustained heatwave conditions for an entire half of the year. Albeit with a markedly reduced likelihood, this holds true even for Tx95p, Tx97.5p, and, with the exception of India & Pakistan, for Tx99p (Supplementary Figs. 110 – 112 ). Observed heatwaves that generated exceptionally large amounts of cumulative heat show projected exceedance likelihoods of 9–13% in Europe, India & Pakistan, and Northern Africa & Middle East under SSP1-2.6 (Supplementary Data 21 ). In South America and Southern Africa the respective cumulative heat is exceeded by ~1-in-5 and 1-in-4 projected heatwaves, respectively. This is the case in only 1-in-50 heatwaves in Australia and China (Supplementary Data 21 ), highlighting the record-nature of these two events. These chances, however, substantially increase under high emissions (SSP3-7.0), where approximately 1-in-8 and 1-in-13 projected heatwaves in Australia and China, respectively, generate more cumulative heat than the observed event (Supplementary Data 22 ). In Europe, India & Pakistan, and Northern Africa & Middle East, projected heatwaves show chances of 20–30% to exceed the exceptionally high cumulative heat. In South America and Southern Africa, this is the case in 30–40% of projected heatwaves (Supplementary Data 22 ). Except for Australia and China, most of the regions that experienced heatwaves with exceptionally high cumulative heat have a chance of approximately 1-in-10 to 1-in-5 heatwaves generating more than twice the respective reference event’s cumulative heat under SSP1-2.6 (Supplementary Data 23 ). Under SSP3-7.0, this increases to approximately 1-in-8 to 1-in-4 projected heatwaves in these regions, whereas Australia and China show a chance of approximately 1-in-5 projected heatwaves (Supplementary Data 24 ).
